newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Compulsory savings could help NZ c/a deficit - Birch.
newsitem.headline: Compulsory savings could help NZ c/a deficit - Birch.

text.p: A proposed compulsory pension savings scheme could help boost growth and address New Zealand's current account deficit, Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Monday.
Birch said New Zealand needed to increase capital stock substantially every year to ensure high, sustained economic growth.
"We do not save enough ourselves to fund our growth rate," he said in a speech to the SBC Warburg Investor Group in Wellington.
Birch said the Reserve Bank was forecasting an average current account deficit of 5.7 percent of GDP in the four years to 1999-2000.

The compulsory pensions scheme proposed by Treasurer Winston Peters was designed in part to address the problem of increasing savings to fund growth, Birch said. "It may help both growth and that deficit."
Peters' New Zealand First party, the junior coalition partner, favours compulsory superannuation, but Birch's National party opposed it during last year's election campaign.
New Zealanders will vote in a September referendum on whether to support compulsory retirement savings.
Birch said even if they backed such a scheme, overseas investment would still make a major contribution to consumer choice, technical know-how, market access and management expertise.
He noted that most of New Zealand's biggest companies were designated as foreign-owned for current account purposes.

"Some of the profits of our biggest, most successful companies, Fletcher Challenge, Brierley, Carter Holt and so on, even if the money never leaves New Zealand, impact negatively on our current account balance," he said.
"The quite substantial sums involved are, on the other hand, offset by a positive impact of equal magnitude, in the Capital Account."
Birch said the current account deficit was private-sector driven and government consumption played no part in it.
